description:
I’m Dahil, a full-stack/backend software developer with a background in Medical Laboratory Techniques and Computer Science.
We are tackling Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions by building OrbitalDx, an autonomous clinical decision-support and telemetry dashboard designed for long-duration missions where communication delays with Earth mean astronauts must detect and manage health risks on their own.
summary:
OrbitoDX is an autonomous clinical decision-support and physiological telemetry platform designed for astronauts on long-duration space missions. Built as a self-contained, offline-first Go web application, it integrates an interactive anatomical body twin, a manual vitals check-in and anomaly simulator, 30-day trend charts, and a Canadian Space Agency (CSA) CANS neutron radiation dosimetry module.
To address the challenge, OrbitoDX maps vital signs, ocular indicators, and radiation exposure directly to NASA Human Research Program’s Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight. It classifies physiological drift into color-coded Green, Amber, and Red triage tiers and provides non-physician crew members with plain-English clinical explanations and step-by-step countermeasure checklists.
This is critical because communication delays on Moon and Mars missions can go up to 20 minutes each way prevent real-time Flight Surgeon intervention. Beyond deep space, OrbitoDX’s lightweight offline architecture translates directly to remote rural clinics on Earth lacking immediate specialist access.
details:
On deep-space missions to the Moon and Mars, astronauts face communication delays with Earth of up to 20 minutes each way. When an astronaut's blood pressure drops, intracranial pressure builds up, or a solar particle event spikes cabin radiation, waiting nearly forty minutes for a round-trip answer from Houston isn't practical. Most crew members are engineers and scientists rather than medical doctors, so they need a fast, offline tool onboard that can interpret vital signs, explain what is happening in plain English, and walk them through what to do next.

That is why we built OrbitoDX, an offline clinical decision-support and health monitoring dashboard for long-duration spaceflight. The system lets crew members switch between mission profiles for example Low Earth Orbit on the ISS, an Artemis Lunar Base, and a Mars Transit spacecraft which automatically adjusts gravity baselines, radiation exposure models, and a live Earth signal-delay timer. Through an interactive anatomical body map, crew members can inspect four key physiological zones: Head and Eyes (tracking Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome and circadian sleep), Heart and Chest (blood pressure, heart rate, and cabin CO₂), Skeleton and Muscles (microgravity bone density loss and resistive exercise compliance), and Blood, Immune, and Radiation. Every reading is mapped directly against NASA's Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight alongside secondary neutron dosimetry modeled on the Canadian Space Agency's CANS research, which shows that neutrons account for roughly thirty percent of crew radiation dose aboard the ISS.

Rather than dumping raw numbers onto a screen, OrbitoDX runs an autonomous triage engine that classifies drift into Green, Amber, or Red tiers. Each alert explains why the exam matters, how spaceflight hazards trigger that specific physiological change, and gives a step-by-step countermeasure checklist using onboard equipment. Crew members can log daily vitals, track 30-day longitudinal trends alongside a daily readiness streak, or trigger simulated emergencies like a Mars solar neutron spike to see how compound hazards interact. We also built in a store-and-forward telemetry packet generator so clinical summaries can be queued for asynchronous transmission back to Flight Surgeons whenever bandwidth opens up.

What makes OrbitoDX practical and creative is both its clinical framing and its engineering footprint. Instead of treating vitals in isolation, it connects compound hazards, such as how radiation and sleep disruption elevate stress cortisol and immune risk and translates them into plain-language protocols any crew member can follow under pressure. Under the hood, we engineered OrbitoDX in Go using Fiber, templ, Tailwind CSS, Alpine.js, and Chart.js, compiling the entire application and its frontend assets into a single self-contained binary with zero reliance on external cloud APIs or internet connectivity. Because it runs completely offline on lightweight hardware, the exact same software can serve remote rural clinics on Earth where medical specialists are hours away.
